topic.subject: chemistry
topic.title: Acids, alkalis, indicators and pH
topic.overview: The pH scale describes how acidic or alkaline a solution is. Indicators change colour so that pH or a broad category can be estimated safely.
learningGoals: Recall the precise Year 8 scientific vocabulary and symbols.
Apply the idea to an unfamiliar example rather than relying on recognition.
Use the command word, show working where needed and include every mark point.
mustMemoriseRules: At Year 8 level, pH below 7 is acidic, pH 7 is neutral and pH above 7 is alkaline.
Universal indicator gives a range: red/orange/yellow acidic, green neutral, blue/purple alkaline.
Blue litmus turns red in acid; red litmus turns blue in alkali.
An alkali is a soluble base; not every base is soluble.
Indicators reveal acidity or alkalinity but do not themselves make a solution safe.
Use a spotting tile or small test samples, eye protection and clean droppers to prevent contamination.

mustMemoriseVocabulary.meaning: a substance that neutralises a base and has pH below 7 in aqueous solution
a substance that neutralises an acid
a soluble base with pH above 7 in aqueous solution
a substance that changes colour depending on pH
a mixture of indicators showing a range of colours across the pH scale
an indicator that distinguishes acids from alkalis
a numerical scale used to describe acidity and alkalinity

workedExamples.answer: pH 3 acid; pH 7 neutral; pH 11 alkali.

workedExamples.prompt: Blue litmus turns red. What does this show?

practicals.title: Make and test a plant indicator
practicals.aim: Prepare a coloured plant extract and compare its colours in known and unknown solutions.
practicals.variables: IV: solution tested; DV: indicator colour; controls: volumes/concentration/indicator amount/lighting.
practicals.method: Crush or warm red cabbage with water, filter, add equal indicator volumes to small samples, record colours and compare with known pH values.
practicals.expectedResult: Acids tend pink/red, neutral near purple and alkalis blue/green; exact shades depend on preparation.
practicals.safety: Wear eye protection, use only laboratory solutions, avoid tasting and prevent cross-contamination.
practicals.evaluation: Repeat borderline colours, use a white background and compare with universal indicator or a pH probe.

examTips: Anchor the scale at 7 before classifying a pH.
Name the starting litmus colour and final colour.
When judging colour data, acknowledge that home-made indicators give approximate pH only.
beforeStartingPractice: Read the key rules once, cover them, then retrieve them aloud or in writing.
Use MC first for confidence, but finish with typed, calculation, practical or explanation evidence.
After an error, study the explanation; the same concept returns later in a different format and again after 2 and 7 days.

practicals.subject: chemistry
practicals.title: Make and test a plant indicator
practicals.aim: Prepare a coloured plant extract and compare its colours in known and unknown solutions.
practicals.variables: IV: solution tested; DV: indicator colour; controls: volumes/concentration/indicator amount/lighting.
practicals.method: Crush or warm red cabbage with water, filter, add equal indicator volumes to small samples, record colours and compare with known pH values.
practicals.expectedResult: Acids tend pink/red, neutral near purple and alkalis blue/green; exact shades depend on preparation.
practicals.safety: Wear eye protection, use only laboratory solutions, avoid tasting and prevent cross-contamination.
practicals.evaluation: Repeat borderline colours, use a white background and compare with universal indicator or a pH probe.
